## The Chemistry of Combustion: Why Petrol in a Diesel Engine Fails Quickly

The scenario described—driving approximately 100 miles on petrol after refueling an empty diesel tank—is physically improbable and mechanically dangerous. To understand why, we must look at the fundamental differences between diesel and gasoline combustion cycles and how modern fuel injection systems manage these processes.

Diesel engines rely on compression ignition. The air-fuel mixture is injected directly into cylinders that have been compressed to extremely high ratios (often 16:1 or higher). This compression raises the temperature of the air sufficiently to ignite the fuel spontaneously upon injection. Gasoline, conversely, has a much lower octane rating and requires a spark plug to initiate combustion because it cannot self-ignite under normal operating pressures without detonating prematurely (knocking).

When you introduce gasoline into a diesel engine, even with a small residual amount of diesel remaining in the tank, the chemical properties of the fuel change the behavior of the entire system. Gasoline lacks the cetane number required for reliable compression ignition. As the engine attempts to run on this mixture, the combustion event becomes inconsistent. Instead of a controlled burn, you often get incomplete combustion or misfires.

The "juddering" mentioned in your experience is likely the result of uneven cylinder firing. Modern diesel engines use complex timing sequences managed by the Engine Control Unit (ECU). The ECU expects fuel to arrive at specific pressure and temperature thresholds. When gasoline enters the high-pressure rail, it may not atomize or vaporize correctly due to its different volatility compared to diesel. This leads to lean burn conditions in some cylinders while others might experience flooding, creating a vibration that is distinct from normal engine idle or load characteristics.

From an engineering perspective, this issue isn't just about performance; it's about mechanical integrity. Diesel fuel acts as a lubricant for the high-pressure fuel pumps and injectors. Gasoline has significantly lower lubricity. Running a diesel engine on gasoline can lead to rapid wear of the lifters, fuel pump gears, and injector nozzles. Furthermore, gasoline is more volatile than diesel. In the hot environment of a combustion chamber designed for heavy fuels, this volatility increases the risk of pre-ignition or even catastrophic piston damage if the mixture detonates before the intended compression stroke peak.

The residual diesel in your tank likely provided enough lubrication and ignition characteristics to keep the engine running for those initial 100 miles, masking the severity of the contamination until the remaining diesel was consumed or diluted beyond a critical threshold. However, this is a race against time. The likelihood of noticing symptoms after exactly 100 miles varies based on factors like ambient temperature, driving load (idle vs. highway), and the exact ratio of fuels mixed.

If you suspect fuel contamination, the only safe course of action is to stop immediately and drain the system. Continuing to drive risks destroying expensive components like the high-pressure common rail pump or CP4/CP3 injectors, which can cost thousands in repairs. There are no software commands or ECU resets that can compensate for the lack of cetane rating or lubricity; the hardware simply cannot operate correctly on the wrong fuel type.

For developers maintaining fleet vehicles or building diagnostic tools, detecting fuel type anomalies often involves monitoring sensor data streams for irregularities in cylinder pressure or injector pulse width. If an engine is running significantly leaner than expected despite full load requests, it may indicate a fuel mismatch rather than just an injector fault.
